When the disciples saw him walking across the lake, they were terrified. “It is a ghost!” they said, and screamed in fear.
But at once Jesus spoke to them: “Take heart; it is I.{g} Do not be afraid.”
Peter answered him, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.”
“Come,” said Jesus. Peter climbed out of the boat and walked on the water, making his way toward Jesus.
But when he saw the wind,{h} he became frightened, and beginning to sink, he cried out, “Lord, save me!”
Jesus immediately reached out his hand and caught hold of him, saying to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”
And when they had climbed into the boat, the wind died down.
Those in the boat bowed down before him and said, “Truly you are the Son of God.”
When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret.{i}
When the men of that place recognized him, they sent word into all that surrounding region and brought to him all who were sick,
and they begged him that they might merely touch the tassel of his cloak; and all who touched it were made completely well.

notes.text: Herod the tetrarch: Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruler of Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. *Tetrarch* (“ruler of a fourth”) was a title for a minor ruler under Rome; Matthew also calls him “king” (verse 9).

Herodias … Philip: Herodias was a granddaughter of Herod the Great. She had been married to her uncle Herod (called Philip here and in Mark 6:17), and left him to marry his half-brother Antipas. Some manuscripts omit “Philip.” The historian Josephus gives a fuller account (*Antiquities* 18.5).
Against the law: Lev 18:16; 20:21.
The daughter of Herodias: named Salome by Josephus.

A long way from land: literally “many stadia from the land.” A stadion was about 607 feet (185 m). The Westcott–Hort text follows Vaticanus here; other manuscripts read “in the middle of the lake.” Compare John 6:19, “about 25 or 30 stadia,” about 3 or 3½ miles (5 or 6 km).
Between three and six in the morning: literally “in the fourth watch of the night.” The Romans divided the night into four watches: about 6–9 p.m., 9 p.m.–midnight, midnight–3 a.m., and 3–6 a.m.
It is I: Greek *egō eimi*, literally “I am,” which may echo God’s self-identification in Exod 3:14 and Isa 43:10.
Saw the wind: the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lacks “strong,” which most manuscripts add.
Gennesaret: a fertile plain on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, between Capernaum and Magdala.

verses.text: Then some Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem with a question:
“What makes your disciples break the tradition handed down by the elders? They do not wash their hands before they eat bread.”{a}
He answered them, “And what makes you break God’s commandment for the sake of your tradition?
God said, ‘Honor your father and mother,’{b} and, ‘Whoever reviles father or mother must certainly be put to death.’{c}
Yet you teach that a person can say to father or mother, ‘Anything of mine that might have helped you is a gift devoted to God,’{d}
he need not honor his father at all. So for the sake of your tradition you have cancelled the word{e} of God.
Hypocrites! Isaiah described you well when he prophesied:
‘This people honors me with their lips, while their heart stays far away from me;
their worship of me is empty, for what they teach as doctrine are human rules.’ ”{f}
Then he called the crowd over and said to them, “Listen, and understand this:
a person is not made unclean by what goes into the mouth; what comes out of the mouth, that is what makes a person unclean.”
Then the disciples came and said to him, “Are you aware that the Pharisees were offended to hear you say this?”
He replied, “Any plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted.
Leave them be. They are blind guides; and when one blind man guides another, the two of them will tumble into a ditch.”{g}
Peter spoke up: “Explain this saying to us.”
“Are you also still slow to grasp it?” Jesus said.
“Do you not see that whatever enters the mouth passes into the stomach and goes out into the latrine?
What comes out of the mouth, though, issues from the heart, and that is what defiles a person.
For from the heart come evil schemes, murders, adulteries, sexual immoralities, thefts, false witness, slanders.
These are what make a person unclean; but eating with hands unwashed does not make anyone unclean.”
Jesus left that area and went to the district of Tyre and Sidon.
And a Canaanite{h} woman from that territory came out and kept crying, “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David! My daughter is tormented by a demon, and it is terrible.”
But he gave her no word of answer. His disciples came to him and urged him, “Send her off; she keeps shouting after us.”
He answered, “I was sent to no one but the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”
But she came and knelt before him. “Lord,” she said, “help me!”
He answered, “It is not right to take bread meant for the children and toss it to the little dogs.”
“True, Lord,” she said, “yet even the little dogs eat the scraps falling from their masters’ table.”
Then Jesus answered her, “Woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you just as you wish.” And her daughter was healed from that hour.
Jesus moved on from there and went along the shore of the Sea of Galilee. He climbed a hillside and sat there.
Great crowds came to him, bringing with them people who were lame, crippled, blind, mute, and many others besides, and laid them at his feet, and he healed them.
The crowd marveled as they saw the mute talking, the maimed restored,{i} the lame walking and the blind seeing, and they praised the God of Israel.

Jesus called his disciples to him and said, “My heart goes out to these people, because for three days now they have stayed with me and they have nothing left to eat. I am not willing to send them away hungry; they might faint on the road.”
His disciples asked him, “Where in this remote place could we find enough bread to feed such a large crowd?”
Jesus asked them, “How many loaves have you got?” They said, “Seven, and a few small fish.”
He instructed the crowd to sit down on the ground,
and he took the seven loaves and the fish, gave thanks, broke them, and kept handing them to the disciples, and the disciples handed them to the crowds.
They all ate their fill, and they collected the broken pieces that remained, seven large baskets full.{j}
There were four thousand men who ate, in addition to women and children.
After dismissing the crowds, he got into the boat and came to the district of Magadan.{k}

notes.text: Wash their hands: ritual washing, not hygiene. The “tradition of the elders” was the body of oral rulings by which the Pharisees applied the Law (compare Mark 7:3–4).
Exod 20:12; Deut 5:16.
A gift devoted to God: something dedicated to God (Mark 7:11 gives the Aramaic term, *Corban*) and therefore, by the rule being criticized, unavailable to support one’s parents.
Word: the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus (corrected) and Vaticanus, reads “word”; some manuscripts read “commandment” and others “law.”
Isa 29:13, quoted in the wording of the Greek Old Testament.
Many later manuscripts read “blind guides of the blind”; the Westcott–Hort text reads simply “blind guides.”
Canaanite: an old biblical name for the non-Israelite peoples of the region; Mark 7:26 calls her “a Greek, Syrophoenician by birth.”
The crippled made whole: the first hand of Sinaiticus and a few other witnesses omit this phrase.
Large baskets: Greek *spyris*, a larger basket than the *kophinos* of 14:20.
Magadan: location uncertain. Later manuscripts read *Magdala*; compare Mark 8:10, “Dalmanutha.”

verses.text: Pharisees and Sadducees approached, testing him, and demanded that he show them some sign out of heaven.
He answered them, [[“When evening comes, you say, ‘Fair weather, for the sky is red’;
and in the morning, ‘Today there will be a storm, because the sky is red and threatening.’ You can interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times.]]{a}
A wicked and adulterous generation clamors for a sign, but it will be given no sign except the sign of Jonah.” Then he left them and went away.
When the disciples reached the far shore, they found that they had forgotten to take bread.
Jesus said to them, “Watch out, and be on guard against the yeast{b} of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”
They discussed this among themselves and said, “He says this because we brought no bread.”
Jesus knew what they were saying and asked, “Why all this talk among yourselves about having no bread, you people of little faith?
Have you not understood yet? Have you forgotten the five loaves that fed five thousand, and the number of baskets you filled with leftovers?
Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many large baskets you gathered?
How can you not understand that I was not speaking about bread? Watch out for the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees!”
Then it dawned on them that he had not told them to beware of the yeast in bread, but of what the Pharisees and Sadducees taught.
When Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi,{c} he put a question to his disciples: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?”
They said, “Some say John the Baptist; others, Elijah; and still others, Jeremiah{d} or one of the prophets.”
He said to them, “And you—who do you say I am?”
Simon Peter spoke up: “You are the Messiah, Son of the living God.”
Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah,{e} for no human being{f} revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven.
And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock{g} I will build my church,{h} and the gates of Hades{i} will not overpower it.
The keys of the kingdom of heaven I will place in your hands. Whatever you bind on earth will already be bound in heaven, and whatever you release on earth will already be released in heaven.”{j}
Then he gave the disciples strict orders not to tell anyone that he was the Messiah.

From then on Jesus{k} started to explain to his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and endure great suffering from the elders, chief priests and scribes, be killed, and rise again on the third day.
Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him: “God have mercy on you,{l} Lord! This must never happen to you!”
But he turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for your thinking is not God’s way of thinking but man’s.”
Then Jesus said to his disciples, “If anyone wants to come after me, let him say no to himself, take up his cross, and follow me.
Anyone set on saving his life{m} will lose it, and anyone who loses his life for my sake will find it.
What will it profit anyone to win the entire world and lose their life? Or what can a person give to get life back?
The Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each person according to their actions.{n}
Amen, I tell you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.”

notes.text: Verses 2b–3 (from “When evening comes” to “the signs of the times”) are absent from Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and other early witnesses, and Jerome knew manuscripts without them. Westcott and Hort enclosed them in double brackets as not part of Matthew’s original text, though very old. They are printed here in double brackets. The Greek *pyrrazei* means “is fiery red.”
Yeast: here a figure for a corrupting influence that spreads unseen (verse 12; compare 1 Cor 5:6–8).

Caesarea Philippi: a town at the foot of Mount Hermon near the source of the Jordan, rebuilt by Herod’s son Philip and named in honor of Caesar Augustus (and to distinguish it from Caesarea on the coast).
Jeremiah: “Yahweh exalts” or “Yahweh throws (down).”
Son of Jonah: Aramaic *Bar-Jona*. John 1:42 and 21:15 call his father John.
No human being: literally “flesh and blood.”
Peter … rock: a wordplay. *Petros* (Peter) and *petra* (rock) are related Greek words, both rendering the Aramaic name *Kepha* (Cephas), “rock” (John 1:42).
Church: Greek *ekklēsia*, “assembly,” used in the Greek Old Testament for the assembly of Israel.
The gates of Hades: the power of death.

Will have been bound … will have been loosed: or “will be bound … will be loosed.” Binding and loosing were rabbinic terms for forbidding and permitting, and also for imposing or lifting a penalty. Compare 18:18.
Jesus: Sinaiticus (first hand) and Vaticanus read “Jesus Christ” here, as does the Westcott–Hort text; most manuscripts read “Jesus.”
God have mercy on you: an idiom meaning “God forbid!”
Life: Greek *psychē*, which can mean “life” or “soul” (also in verse 26).

verses.text: After six days Jesus brought Peter, James, and his brother John up a high mountain by themselves.
And he was transformed before them; his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became as white as the light.
And suddenly Moses and Elijah{a} appeared to them, talking with him.
Peter responded to Jesus, “Lord, it is good that we are here. If you wish, I will put up three shelters{b} here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”
He was still speaking when a bright cloud spread its shadow over them, and out of the cloud a voice said, “This is my Son, my beloved, in whom I delight. Listen to him!”{c}
At the sound of it the disciples fell face down on the ground, overcome with fear.
But Jesus came and touched them. “Get up,” he said, “and do not be afraid.”
When they raised their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus himself, alone.
As they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus ordered them, “Tell no one what you have seen until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.”
The disciples asked him, “Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”
He replied, “Elijah is indeed coming, and he will set everything right again.{d}
But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they pleased. In the same way the Son of Man is about to suffer at their hands.”
Then it became clear to the disciples that he had been talking to them about John the Baptist.
When they reached the crowd, a man came up to Jesus and fell on his knees before him.
and said, “Lord, take pity on my son. He has seizures{e} and is in terrible pain; he often falls into the fire and often into the water.
I brought him to your disciples, but they had no power to cure him.”
Jesus replied, “O faithless and twisted generation!{f} How long shall I remain with you? How long shall I bear with you? Bring the boy to me here.”
Jesus spoke sternly to the demon, and it left the boy; from that hour he was well.
Afterward the disciples came to Jesus privately and asked, “Why were we not able to drive it out?”

“Because you have so little faith,” he told them. “Amen, I tell you, if you have faith no bigger than a grain of mustard seed, you will tell this mountain, ‘Go over there,’ and over there it will go. Nothing will be impossible for you.”
While they were gathering{h} in Galilee, Jesus said to them, “The Son of Man is about to be handed over into human hands,
They will put him to death, and on the third day he will be raised up.” And the disciples were deeply saddened.
After they arrived in Capernaum, the men who collected the temple tax{i} came to Peter. “Your teacher pays the temple tax, doesn’t he?” they asked.

“Yes, he does,” Peter said. When he came into the house, Jesus spoke first: “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth collect tolls or tribute? From their own sons, or from others?”
When Peter said, “From others,” Jesus told him, “Then the sons are exempt.

However, so that we do not offend them, go to the lake and throw in a fishhook. Take the first fish that bites, open its mouth, and you will find a silver coin{j} to cover the tax for both of us. Take it and pay them for you and me.”

notes.text: Moses and Elijah: representing the Law and the Prophets. Both had met God on a mountain (Exod 24; 33–34; 1 Kgs 19). *Moses* is explained in Exod 2:10 as “drawn out.”
Shelters: Greek *skēnē*, “tent,” “booth,” perhaps recalling the booths of the Feast of Tabernacles (Lev 23:42) or the tabernacle in the wilderness.
Compare Ps 2:7; Isa 42:1; Deut 18:15; and 3:17.
Mal 4:5–6 (3:23–24 in Hebrew).
Has seizures: literally “is moonstruck” (Greek *selēniazetai*), a term for epilepsy-like attacks, blamed on the moon.
Faithless and perverse generation: compare Deut 32:5, 20.

The Westcott–Hort text and the earliest manuscripts (including Sinaiticus, first hand, and Vaticanus) do not include verse 21, and the number is kept here only to preserve the traditional verse numbering. Many later manuscripts add, from Mark 9:29, “But this kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting.”
Gathering: the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, reads *systrephomenōn*, “gathering together”; most manuscripts read “staying.”
The temple tax: literally “the two drachmas,” the half-shekel paid yearly by every Jewish man for the upkeep of the temple (Exod 30:13–16; Neh 10:32), equal to about two days’ wages.
A silver coin: Greek *statēr*, a coin worth four drachmas, enough to pay the temple tax for two people.

verses.text: At that time the disciples came to Jesus with the question, “Who, then, ranks highest in the kingdom of heaven?”
He called a little child over, stood the child among them,
and said, “Amen, I tell you, if you do not turn around and become as little children are, there is no way you will enter the kingdom of heaven.
So whoever takes the lowly place of this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.
And whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me.
“But whoever leads astray one of these little ones who trust in me would be better off with a large millstone{a} tied around their neck and drowned in the deep sea.
Alas for the world because of its snares! Snares there must be; but alas for the one through whom the snare comes!

If your hand or your foot leads you into sin, cut it off and throw it from you. Better for you to enter life maimed or lame than to keep both hands or both feet and be thrown into the everlasting fire.
And if your eye causes you to sin, pull it out and throw it away. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than to be thrown into the fire of Gehenna with two.
“Take care that you do not look down on one of these little ones; for I tell you that in heaven their angels are always looking upon the face of my Father in heaven.{b}
What is your opinion? If a man has a hundred sheep and one of them wanders off, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hillsides and go in search of the stray?
And if he happens to find it, amen, I tell you, he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine that never wandered.
In the same way, it is not the will of your{d} Father in heaven that a single one of these little ones should be lost.
“If your brother sins{e} against you, go to him privately and show him where he went wrong, just the two of you. If he pays attention to you, you have won your brother back.
But if he will not listen, take one or two others along with you, so that ‘on the evidence of two or three witnesses every matter may be settled.’{f}
If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the church;{g} and if he refuses to listen even to the church, treat him as you would a Gentile or a tax collector.
Amen, I tell you, whatever you prohibit{h} on earth will already be prohibited in heaven, and whatever you allow on earth will already be allowed in heaven.
Once more, amen, I tell you: when two of you here on earth are of one mind about any request they make, my Father in heaven will do it for them.
For where two or three have come together in my name, there I am in their midst.”
Then Peter came up and asked him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me and I forgive him? Up to seven times?”
“Not up to seven times, I say to you,” Jesus replied, “but up to seventy-seven times.{i}
“For this reason the kingdom of heaven is like a king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants.
When he began the reckoning, a man was brought to him who owed ten thousand bags of silver.{j}
Since he had no means of paying, his master ordered that he be sold, together with his wife and children and everything he owned, and the debt repaid.
So the slave fell down and lay prostrate before him, pleading, ‘Be patient with me, and I will pay you everything.’
Moved with pity, the master of that slave released him and canceled the debt.
But that same slave went out and came upon one of his fellow slaves who owed him a hundred days’ wages.{k} He seized him by the throat and began choking him, saying, ‘Pay up what you owe!’
His fellow slave fell down and begged him, ‘Be patient with me, and I will pay you.’
But he would not hear of it; instead he went off and had him thrown into prison until he should pay the debt.
When his fellow slaves saw what had happened, they were deeply distressed, and they went and reported the whole affair to their master.
Then the master summoned him and said to him, ‘You wicked slave! I canceled that entire debt of yours because you begged me.
Ought you not to have shown mercy to your fellow slave, as I showed mercy to you?’
And in anger his master handed him over to the jailers{l} until he should repay everything owed.
That is how my heavenly Father will deal with each of you, unless you forgive your brother from your heart.”

notes.text: Heavy millstone: literally “a donkey’s millstone,” the large upper stone of a mill turned by a donkey.
Compare Ps 34:7; 91:11; Heb 1:14.

The Westcott–Hort text and the earliest manuscripts (including Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and the Greek of the early versions) do not include verse 11; the number is kept here only to preserve the traditional verse numbering. Many later manuscripts add, from Luke 19:10, “For the Son of Man came to save the lost.”
Your: some manuscripts, including Vaticanus, read “my.”
If your brother sins: most manuscripts add “against you”; the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, omits it (WH prints it in the margin).
Deut 19:15.
Church: Greek *ekklēsia*, “assembly” (see 16:18 note), here the local community of disciples.
Forbid … permit: literally “bind … loose”; see 16:19 note.
Seventy-seven times: or “seventy times seven.” The Greek is ambiguous, but it matches Gen 4:24 in the Greek Old Testament, where Lamech boasts of revenge “seventy-seven times.”

Ten thousand bags of silver: literally “ten thousand talents.” A talent was a weight of silver of about 75 pounds (34 kg), worth about 6,000 denarii, that is, about 6,000 days’ wages for a laborer. The sum is deliberately beyond all reckoning: some 60 million days’ wages. Ten thousand (*myrioi*) was the largest number in Greek counting.
A hundred days’ wages: the Greek says “a hundred denarii,” and a denarius was what a laborer typically earned in a day (20:2). The debt was about one six-hundred-thousandth of the first.
Jailers: or “torturers” (Greek *basanistai*).

verses.text: Once Jesus had ended these sayings, he departed from Galilee and went to the part of Judea that lies across the Jordan.
Great crowds followed him, and he healed them there.
Some Pharisees came to him to test him. “Is it permissible,” they asked, “for a man to divorce his wife on any ground whatever?”
He answered, “Have you not read that the Creator at the beginning made them male and female,{a}
and said, ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two will become one flesh’?{b}
So they are no longer two, but one flesh. What God has yoked together, then, no human being must separate.”
They asked him, “Then why did Moses order that a man give his wife a divorce certificate and send her away?”{c}
He told them, “It was because your hearts were hard that Moses allowed you to divorce your wives; but it was not that way from the beginning.
I tell you, anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another commits adultery.”{d}
The disciples said to him, “If that is how things stand between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry.”
He answered, “This saying is not for everyone to take in, but only for those who are given it.

Some are eunuchs because they were born that way; some were made eunuchs by other people; and some have renounced marriage{e} for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Whoever can take this in should take it in.”
Then little children were brought to him so that he might lay his hands on them and pray. The disciples scolded those who brought them,
but Jesus said, “Let the little children be, and do not stop them from coming to me; for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.”
He laid his hands on them and went on from there.
And now a man came up to him and asked, “Teacher, what good deed must I do to gain eternal life?”
“Why are you asking me about the good?” Jesus replied. “Only One is good.{f} If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments.”
“Which ones?” he asked. Jesus replied, “ ‘You are not to murder, not to commit adultery, not to steal, and not to give false testimony;
honor your father and mother;’{g} and, ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ ”{h}
“All of those I have observed,” the young man told him. “Where do I still fall short?”
Jesus said to him, “If you want to be complete,{i} go and sell what you own and give the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.”
When the young man heard this, he went away grieving, for he had many possessions.
Then Jesus said to his disciples, “Amen, I tell you, it will be hard for someone rich to enter the kingdom of heaven.
And again I say to you, a camel could go through the eye of a needle{j} more easily than a rich person could enter the kingdom of God.”
When the disciples heard this, they were utterly astonished. “Who then can be saved?” they asked.
Looking at them, Jesus said, “For human beings it is impossible, but for God everything is possible.”{k}
Then Peter answered him, “We have given up everything and followed you. What will we get?”

Jesus answered them, “Amen, I tell you: at the world’s rebirth,{l} when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his glory, you who followed me will likewise sit on twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel.
And everyone who has given up houses, brothers, sisters, father, mother,{m} children or fields for the sake of my name will receive a hundred times as much{n} and inherit eternal life.
Yet many now first will be last, and many now last will be first.

notes.text: Except for sexual unfaithfulness: Greek *porneia*, a broad term for sexual immorality, whose exact sense here is debated. Compare 5:32. Many manuscripts add, from 5:32, “and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery”; the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and other witnesses, lacks it (WH prints it in the margin).

Renounced marriage: literally “made themselves eunuchs.” Eunuchs were men who could not father children. Those who “made themselves eunuchs” are generally understood as those who chose to remain unmarried for the sake of the kingdom.

Why are you asking me about the good? Only One is good: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Most later manuscripts assimilate to Mark 10:17–18: “Good teacher … Why do you call me good? No one is good but One, that is, God.”
Complete: or “perfect” (compare 5:48).
A camel … the eye of a needle: a proverbial image of something impossible. Compare the rabbinic proverb of an elephant going through the eye of a needle.
Compare Gen 18:14; Job 42:2; Zech 8:6.
The world’s rebirth: Greek *palingenesia*, “new genesis” or “rebirth,” the renewal of the world at the end of the age.
Mother: most manuscripts add “or wife”; the Westcott–Hort text, with Vaticanus and other witnesses, lacks it.
Many times as much: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Vaticanus and a few other witnesses; most manuscripts read “a hundred times as much.”

verses.text: “For the kingdom of heaven is like a landowner who went out at daybreak to hire laborers for his vineyard.
He agreed with the laborers to pay them the usual day’s wage{a} and sent them into his vineyard.
Going out again at about nine in the morning,{b} he saw others standing idle in the marketplace,
and he said to them, ‘You too go into the vineyard, and I will give you whatever is fair.’ So off they went.
He went out again around noon and again around three in the afternoon, and did the same.
About five o’clock in the afternoon he went out again and found others standing around. He asked them, ‘Why are you standing here idle all day long?’
‘Because no one has hired us,’ they answered. He told them, ‘You also go to the vineyard.’
When evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his manager, ‘Call the laborers and pay them their wages, starting with the last and ending with the first.’
Those hired at about five o’clock came, and each received a full day’s wage.
So when the first came, they supposed they would receive more; but each of them, too, received a day’s wage.
On receiving it, they began grumbling against the landowner:
‘These latecomers put in one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat.’
But he answered one of them, ‘Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me on a day’s wage?
Take what is yours and go. I choose to give this last man the same as I give you.
Do I not have the right to do what I want with what is mine? Are you envious because I am generous?’{c}
So the last will be first, and the first last.”{d}
As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the Twelve aside by themselves, and on the road he said to them,
“Listen: we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes. They will sentence him to death
and hand him on to the Gentiles, who will make sport of him, whip him and crucify him; and on the third day he will be raised up.”
Then the mother of Zebedee’s sons came to him with her sons, bowing down and asking a favor of him.
“What would you like?” he asked. She answered, “Give your word that in your kingdom these two sons of mine will sit beside you, the one on your right and the other on your left.”
Jesus answered, “You do not know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup{e} that I am about to drink?” “We can,” they said.{f}
He told them, “You will drink my cup, yes; but the seats at my right and left are not mine to give. They are for those for whom my Father has made them ready.”
When the other ten heard about this, they were indignant with the two brothers.
But Jesus called them to him and said, “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great men make them feel their authority.
It must not be like that among you. Whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant,
and whoever wishes to be first among you must be your slave,
just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom{g} for many.”
As they made their way out of Jericho,{h} a great crowd went along with him.
Two blind men sitting by the roadside heard that Jesus was passing and shouted, “Lord, Son of David, have pity on us!”
The people scolded them and told them to hush, but they cried out even more loudly, “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!”
Jesus came to a halt and called out to them, “What would you have me do for you?”
“Lord,” they answered, “we want our eyes opened.”
Jesus was filled with pity and touched their eyes, and at once their sight came back, and they followed him.

notes.text: The usual day’s wage: literally “a denarius for the day.” The denarius was a Roman silver coin, the normal daily pay of a laborer; so also in verses 9, 10 and 13.

About nine in the morning: literally “about the third hour.” The day was counted from sunrise (about 6 a.m.), so the sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m., and the eleventh (verses 6 and 9) about 5 p.m.
Is your eye evil because I am good: an idiom. An “evil eye” means envy or stinginess (compare 6:23), so: “Are you envious because I am generous?”
Many manuscripts add, from 22:14, “For many are called, but few are chosen”; the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lacks it.
Cup: a figure for suffering appointed by God (compare 26:39; Isa 51:17; Jer 25:15).

Many manuscripts add, from Mark 10:38–39, “or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized,” and in verse 23 “and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized”; the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and others, lacks both.
Ransom: Greek *lytron*, the price paid to free a slave or captive. Compare Isa 53:10–12.
Jericho: an ancient city near the Jordan, about 15 miles (24 km) northeast of Jerusalem, rebuilt by Herod the Great. The name may mean “moon city” or “fragrant.”

verses.text: As they approached Jerusalem and reached Bethphage{a} on the Mount of Olives,{b} Jesus dispatched two of his disciples
and told them, “Go to the village ahead of you. Right when you enter it, you will find a tied donkey and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me.
And if anyone says anything to you, you shall say, ‘The Lord needs them,’ and he will send them at once.”
All this happened so that the word spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled:
“Say to the daughter of Zion,{c} ‘See, your king is coming to you, gentle, and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.’ ”{d}
The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them.
They led the donkey and the colt back, laid their cloaks over them, and he took his seat on them.{e}
Very many in the crowd laid their own cloaks on the road, and others were cutting branches off the trees and laying them on the road.
The crowds that went ahead of him and those that followed kept shouting, “Hosanna{f} to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!{g} Hosanna in the highest heaven!”
When he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was shaken. “Who is this?” people asked.
The crowds answered, “This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth in Galilee.”
Jesus entered the temple{h} and threw out everyone doing business there, sellers and buyers alike; he tipped over the money changers’ tables and the chairs of the dove sellers.{i}
He said to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’{j} but you are making it a den of robbers.”{k}
Blind and lame people came to him in the temple, and he healed them.
But the chief priests and the scribes were incensed when they saw the marvels he performed and heard the children in the temple calling out, “Hosanna to the Son of David!”
and asked him, “Do you hear what they are saying?” Jesus answered, “Yes. Have you never read: ‘From the mouths of children and infants you have prepared praise’?”{l}
And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany{m} and spent the night there.
Early in the morning, as he was going back to the city, he was hungry.
Seeing a fig tree by the road, he went to it and found nothing on it but leaves. He said to it, “May fruit never come from you again!” And the fig tree withered at once.
The disciples were astonished at the sight. “How did the fig tree dry up all at once?” they asked.

Jesus said in reply, “Amen, I tell you, if you have faith and are not of two minds, you will do not only what I did to the fig tree; you could even tell this mountain, ‘Up with you, and into the sea!’ and so it would be.
And whatever you ask for in prayer, believing, you will receive.”

When he had entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came to him as he was teaching and said, “By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?”
Jesus replied, “I have one question for you as well. Answer me, and I will tell you on what authority I act as I do.
John’s baptism: where did it come from? From heaven, or from human beings?” They argued it out among themselves: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’
And if we say, ‘Of human origin,’ we have the people to fear, since everyone takes John for a prophet.”
So their answer to Jesus was, “We cannot tell.” He in turn said to them, “Then neither am I telling you on what authority I act as I do.
“Now tell me what you think. A man who had two sons went to the first and said, ‘My son, go and put in a day’s work in the vineyard.’
‘I am going, sir,’ he replied; but he never went.
The father went to the second son and said the same thing. He answered, ‘I will not,’ but afterward he changed his mind and went.
Which of the two did what his father wanted?” “The second,”{n} they answered. Jesus said to them, “Amen, I tell you, tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom of God ahead of you.

For John came to you showing the way of righteousness, and you put no faith in him; yet tax collectors and prostitutes put their faith in him. You saw that, and even so you did not repent afterward and believe him.
“Hear another parable. A certain householder planted a vineyard, hedged it about, hollowed out a winepress in it and put up a tower.{o} Then he rented it out to growers and left the country.
As the season of fruit came near, he sent his slaves to the growers to receive his share of the crop.
But the growers seized his slaves; one they beat, another they killed, another they stoned.
He sent still other servants, a larger group than before, and the tenants treated these in the same way.
Last of all he sent them his son. ‘My son they will respect,’ he said.
But when the growers saw the son, they said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and seize his inheritance.’
And they took him, threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him.
So when the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those growers?”
They answered, “He will put those villains to a miserable death and rent the vineyard out to other growers, who will hand over his share of the fruit when it is due.”
Jesus said to them, “Did you never read in the Scriptures, ‘The stone the builders threw aside has been made the head of the corner;{p} this is the Lord’s doing, and a wonder in our eyes’?{q}
That is why I say to you that God’s kingdom will be taken from you and handed to a nation that yields its fruit.
[Anyone who falls on this stone will be shattered, and anyone on whom it falls will be ground to powder.]{r}
Hearing his parables, the chief priests and the Pharisees knew that he was talking about them.
They were eager to lay hands on him, but were afraid of the crowds, who held him to be a prophet.

notes.text: Bethphage: “house of unripe figs,” a village on the Mount of Olives near Bethany.
Mount of Olives: the ridge east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley. Compare Zech 14:4.
Daughter of Zion: a poetic name for Jerusalem and its people. *Zion* was the hill of the city of David.
Isa 62:11; Zech 9:9.
He sat on them: that is, on the cloaks.
Hosanna: from Hebrew *hoshi‘ah na’*, “save, please!” (Ps 118:25), which by this time had become a shout of praise.
Ps 118:26. “The Lord” translates *kyrios*, which in the Hebrew is the divine name Yahweh.

The temple: Greek *hieron*, the whole temple complex. The selling and money changing took place in the outer court, the Court of the Gentiles. Many manuscripts read “the temple of God”; the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, reads “the temple.”
Money changers … doves: the temple tax had to be paid in Tyrian silver, so other coins were exchanged; doves were the offering of the poor (Lev 5:7; 12:8).
Ps 8:2 (8:3 in Hebrew), quoted in the wording of the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew reads “you have established strength.”
Bethany: a village about 2 miles (3 km) from Jerusalem on the far side of the Mount of Olives. The name may mean “house of the poor” or “house of Ananiah.”

The second: literally “the latter.” The manuscripts differ widely in verses 29–31. Many read the order: the first son says “I will not” but goes, and the second says “I will, sir” but does not go, with the answer “the first.” The Westcott–Hort text follows Vaticanus and others in the order given here. Codex Bezae (D) has the father’s will done by the son who says no, yet answers “the latter,” which makes little sense. Scholarly review recommended.
The head of the corner: either the foundation stone at a corner or the capstone.
Ps 118:22–23. “The Lord” is Yahweh in the Hebrew.

Verse 44 is absent from Codex Bezae (D), some Old Latin manuscripts, and early writers, and may have been added from Luke 20:18. It is present in Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, and the Westcott–Hort text prints it in single brackets as doubtful. It is printed here in brackets. Compare Isa 8:14–15; Dan 2:34–35, 44–45.

verses.text: Once more Jesus spoke to them in parables. He said:
“Here is a picture of the kingdom of heaven: a king held a marriage feast in honor of his son.
He dispatched his slaves to call the guests who had been invited to the feast, but they refused to come.
Then he sent other slaves, telling them, ‘Say to the invited guests: Look, my dinner is prepared; my oxen and fattened cattle are slaughtered, and everything stands ready. Come to the wedding.’
But they shrugged it off and went their ways, this one to his farm and that one to his business,
while the rest laid hold of his slaves, mistreated them, and killed them.
The king was furious. He sent his troops, destroyed those murderers, and set their city on fire.
Then he said to his slaves, ‘The wedding is ready, but the invited guests did not deserve it.
So go out to where the roads leave the city{a} and invite to the wedding as many as you can find.’
Out went those slaves into the roads and brought in everyone they came across, bad and good alike, and the wedding hall was crowded with guests.
“When the king came in to view the guests, he caught sight of a man there who had on no wedding garment.
‘My friend,’ he asked, ‘how did you get in here without wedding clothes?’ The man had no answer.
Then the king told his attendants, ‘Bind his hands and feet and throw him out into the darkness, where there will be weeping and grinding of teeth.’
For many are called, but few are chosen.”
Then the Pharisees went and laid plans to trap him in what he said.

They sent their disciples to him along with the Herodians,{b} who said, “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth, and you defer to no one, for you pay no regard to a person’s standing.
So give us your opinion: is it lawful to pay the poll tax{c} to Caesar, or not?”
Jesus saw through their malice and said, “Hypocrites! Why are you putting me to the test?
Let me see the coin you pay the tax with.” And they brought him a silver coin.{d}
He asked them, “Whose likeness is this, and whose inscription?”
“Caesar’s,” they told him. He said to them, “Then pay to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and pay to God what belongs to God.”
Hearing this, they were astonished; and leaving him, they departed.
That same day some Sadducees came to him, who say there is no resurrection,{e} and they put a question to him:
“Teacher, Moses said, ‘If a man dies without children, his brother is to marry the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.’{f}
Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and having no offspring, he left his wife to his brother.
So too the second and the third, all the way to the seventh.
Last of all the woman died.
In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be of the seven? For they all had her.”
Jesus answered them, “You are going astray, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God.
In the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.
And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what God said to you:
‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob’?{g} He is not a God of dead people, but of living ones.”
When the crowds heard this, they were astounded at his teaching.
When the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together,
and a lawyer{h} among them tried to trip him up by asking,
“Teacher, which commandment in the Law is greatest?”
Jesus said to him, “ ‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’{i}
This is the great and first commandment.
And there is a second resembling it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’{j}
On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets hang.”
While the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question:
“How do you see the Messiah? Whose descendant is he?” “David’s,” they answered.
He asked them, “Then how can David, inspired by the Spirit, call him Lord? For he says,
‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet’?{k}
If, then, David calls him Lord, in what sense is he David’s son?”
No one was able to give him a word in answer, and from that day no one dared to question him any further.

notes.text: Where the roads leave the city: literally “the outlets of the roads,” where the city streets ran out into the open country, or the crossroads.
Herodians: supporters of the dynasty of Herod, and so of cooperation with Rome.
Poll tax: Greek *kēnsos* (Latin *census*), the head tax paid by every adult to Rome, bitterly resented by many Jews.
A silver coin: literally “a denarius,” a Roman silver coin worth a day’s wage, bearing the image of the emperor Tiberius and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus.
Sadducees: see 3:7 note. They accepted only the Law of Moses as binding and denied a future resurrection (Acts 23:8).
Deut 25:5–6; compare Gen 38:8. This is the custom of “levirate” marriage.
A lawyer: that is, an expert in the Law of Moses; Greek *nomikos*, a specialist in the Law of Moses, much the same as a scribe. A few witnesses omit the word.
Deut 6:5, where “the Lord” is Yahweh in the Hebrew. The Hebrew has “heart … soul … strength”; Matthew gives “mind” for the last.
Ps 110:1. In the Hebrew, “The Lord said” is “Yahweh said”; “my Lord” is *adoni*, “my master.” Many manuscripts read “a footstool for your feet,” as in the Greek Old Testament.

verses.text: Then Jesus addressed the crowds and his disciples:
“The scribes and the Pharisees sit in the chair of Moses.{a}
So do whatever they tell you, and keep it; but do not imitate their actions, for they talk but do not act.
They tie up heavy loads and pile them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves will not lift a finger to shift them.
All their deeds they do to be noticed by others; they make their phylacteries{b} broad and the tassels on their garments long;
they love the places of honor at banquets and the front seats in the synagogues,
and being greeted respectfully in the marketplaces, and being called Rabbi{c} by people.
You, though, are not to be addressed as Rabbi; your teacher is One, and all of you are brothers.
And call no one on earth your father, for you have one Father, the heavenly one.
Nor must you be called leaders, for you have one leader, the Messiah.
The greatest among you will be your servant.
Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.
“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You lock people out of the kingdom of heaven. You do not enter yourselves, and when others are going in, you will not let them.
“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You travel over sea and dry land to make a single convert,{e} and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves.
“Woe to you, blind guides, who say, ‘If anyone swears by the sanctuary,{f} it means nothing; but if anyone swears by the gold of the sanctuary, he is bound by his oath.’
Blind fools! Which is greater, the gold, or the sanctuary that made the gold sacred?
And you say, ‘If anyone swears by the altar, it means nothing; but if anyone swears by the gift that is on it, he is bound.’
Blind people! Which is greater, the gift, or the altar that makes the gift sacred?
So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it;
and to swear by the sanctuary is to swear by it and by the one who lives in it;
and whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits on it.

“How terrible for you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You give a tenth of your mint, dill and cumin,{g} but you have ignored the more important matters of the Law: justice, mercy and faithfulness. You should have done these things without ignoring the others.
Blind guides! You strain out a gnat and gulp down a camel!{h}
“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You clean the outside of the cup and the dish, but inside they are full of plunder and self-indulgence.
Blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup [and the dish],{i} so that the outside of it may become clean as well.
“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You resemble tombs coated with whitewash,{j} handsome to look at from outside, but full within of the bones of the dead and of all that is unclean.
In the same way you too look righteous to people on the outside, but inside you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness.
“How terrible for you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You build tombs for the prophets and decorate the graves of the righteous,
and you say, ‘If we had lived in the time of our ancestors, we would never have taken part with them in killing the prophets.’
So you testify against yourselves that you are the sons of those who murdered the prophets.
Go on, then, fill up the measure your fathers began!
You snakes, you brood of vipers, how will you escape being sentenced to Gehenna?
For this reason, look, I am sending you prophets and wise men and scribes. Some of them you will kill and crucify, and some you will flog in your synagogues and hunt from town to town;

so that upon you may come all the righteous blood shed on the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah,{k} whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar.
Amen, I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation.

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to her! How often have I longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing.
Look, your house is left to you.{l}
For I tell you, you will not see me from now on until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’ ”{m}

notes.text: The chair of Moses: the seat of authority to teach and interpret the Law. Synagogues had a stone seat of this name.

Phylacteries: small leather boxes containing passages of Scripture (Exod 13:1–16; Deut 6:4–9; 11:13–21), worn on the forehead and arm during prayer (compare Deut 6:8). Tassels: see Num 15:38–39 and 9:20 note.
Rabbi: Hebrew/Aramaic for “my great one,” “my master,” used as a title of respect for a teacher.

The Westcott–Hort text and the earliest manuscripts (including Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae and others) do not include verse 14; the number is kept here only to preserve the traditional verse numbering. Many later manuscripts add, from Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47 (and some place it before verse 13), “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you devour widows’ houses and for a pretense make long prayers; therefore you will receive the greater condemnation.”
Convert: Greek *prosēlytos*, a Gentile who had accepted circumcision and the Law of Moses.
Sanctuary: Greek *naos*, the temple building itself, as distinct from the whole complex (*hieron*); also in verses 17, 21 and 35.
Mint and dill and cumin: garden herbs. The Law required a tenth of produce (Lev 27:30; Deut 14:22–23); the Pharisees applied it even to small herbs.
Gnat … camel: a joke. Both were unclean animals (Lev 11:4, 20–23); in Aramaic the words sound alike (*qalma*, *gamla*).
And the dish: printed in brackets in the Westcott–Hort text as doubtful; Codex Bezae and a few other witnesses omit it.
Whitewashed tombs: tombs were whitewashed so that people would not touch them unawares and become ritually unclean (Num 19:16).

Abel … Zechariah: Abel is the first murder victim in the Bible (Gen 4:8), and Zechariah son of Jehoiada the last in the Hebrew order of the books, which ends with Chronicles (2 Chr 24:20–22). Matthew’s “son of Barachiah” may reflect the prophet Zechariah (Zech 1:1). Sinaiticus (first hand) omits “son of Barachiah.” *Abel* means “breath,” “vapor”; *Zechariah* means “Yahweh remembers.”
Left to you: many manuscripts add “desolate,” as does the Westcott–Hort margin; Vaticanus and a few others lack it. Compare Jer 12:7; 22:5.
Ps 118:26, where “the Lord” is Yahweh in the Hebrew.

verses.text: As Jesus came out of the temple and was going on his way, his disciples approached to direct his attention to the temple buildings.
He replied, “You see all this, do you not? Amen, I tell you, here not one stone will be left standing on another; every stone will be torn down.”
While he was seated on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him by themselves. “Tell us,” they said, “when is this to be, and what sign will mark your coming{a} and the close of the age?”
Jesus answered them, “See that no one leads you astray.
Many will come using my name and claiming, ‘I am the Messiah,’ and they will deceive many.
You will hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you are not alarmed; these things must happen, but the end is not yet.
Nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom,{b} and there will be famines and earthquakes in one place after another.
All this is only the first of the labor pains.{c}
“Then they will hand you over to be tormented and will kill you, and you will be hated by all nations because of my name.
At that time many will be tripped up; they will hand each other over and hate each other.
Many false prophets will arise and lead many astray.
And because lawlessness will increase, the love of most people will grow cold.
But whoever endures to the end will be saved.
And this good news of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole inhabited world as a testimony to all the nations, and then the end will come.
“So when you see the desolating abomination{d} spoken of by Daniel the prophet standing in the holy place (let the reader understand),
then let those who are in Judea escape into the mountains.
Anyone on the housetop must not go down to take anything out of his house,
and anyone in the field must not turn back to fetch his cloak.
How dreadful it will be in those days for expectant mothers and for women with nursing babies!
Pray that your flight may not come in winter or on a Sabbath.
For then there will be great distress, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, and never will be again.{e}
Unless those days were shortened, no living thing would be rescued; but for the elect’s sake those days will be shortened.
At that time, if someone tells you, ‘The Messiah is here!’ or ‘He is over there!’ put no faith in it.
For false messiahs and false prophets will arise and produce great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the chosen.
There, I have told you beforehand.
So if people tell you, ‘He is out in the wilderness,’ stay where you are; if they say, ‘He is in the back rooms,’ put no faith in it.
Like lightning that flashes out of the east and lights up the sky to the west, so the coming of the Son of Man will be.
Where the corpse lies, the vultures{f} flock together.
“Immediately after the distress of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.{g}

Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn,{h} and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.{i}
With a great trumpet blast{j} he will send forth his angels, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one edge of the heavens to the other.
“Let the fig tree teach you its lesson. When its branch turns soft and its leaves sprout, you recognize that summer is close.
In the same way, when you see all this happening, recognize that he is close, right at the door.
Amen, I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.
Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.
“As for that day and hour, nobody knows it, not the angels of heaven, not the Son,{k} only the Father.
For as the days of Noah were, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.
For as in those days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark,
and they were unaware until the flood came and carried every one of them off; that is how the Son of Man’s coming will be.{l}
Then two men will be in the field; one is taken and one is left.
Two women will be grinding at the mill; one is taken and one is left.
Stay alert, therefore, since you cannot know the day of your Lord’s coming.
Understand this: if the householder had known in which part of the night{m} the thief would come, he would have kept watch and not allowed his house to be dug through.
That is why you also must stand ready; the Son of Man will come at an hour when you are not looking for him.
“Who, then, is the trustworthy and prudent slave, set by his master over the household staff to give them their rations at the right time?
Happy that slave, if his master finds him so engaged when he arrives!
Amen, I tell you, his master will make him steward of everything he owns.
But suppose that slave is wicked and thinks, ‘My master is taking his time,’
and he starts beating his fellow slaves and feasting and drinking with drunkards;
then that slave’s master will arrive on a day he does not foresee and at an hour he is not aware of,
and cut him to pieces,{n} and give him a place among the hypocrites, where there will be weeping and grinding of teeth.

notes.text: Coming: Greek *parousia*, “presence,” “arrival,” used of the visit of a king or high official; also in verses 27, 37 and 39.
Compare Isa 19:2; 2 Chr 15:6.
Labor pains: a common image for the sufferings expected to come before the age to come.

The desolating abomination: traditionally “the abomination of desolation,” a sacrilege that makes the holy place desolate. Dan 9:27; 11:31; 12:11. Daniel refers to the pagan altar set up in the temple by Antiochus IV in 167 BC (1 Macc 1:54).
Compare Dan 12:1; Joel 2:2.
Vultures: Greek *aetoi*, usually “eagles,” but here carrion birds.
Isa 13:10; 34:4; compare Ezek 32:7; Joel 2:10.
Compare Zech 12:10–14.
A great trumpet blast: compare Isa 27:13. Some manuscripts read “a trumpet and a loud sound.”

Nor the Son: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus (first hand), Bezae and others; most later manuscripts lack these words, perhaps because they seemed to limit the Son’s knowledge. Compare Mark 13:32.
In which part of the night: literally “in which watch.” The night was divided into watches (see 14:25 note).
Cut him in pieces: or “punish him severely.”

verses.text: “At that time the kingdom of heaven will be compared to ten young bridesmaids{a} who took their lamps and set out to meet the groom.
Five of them were foolish, and five were sensible.
The foolish ones took their lamps but brought no oil along;
the sensible ones took flasks of oil with their lamps.
Since the bridegroom was delayed, they all nodded off and slept.
But at midnight a shout rang out: ‘The bridegroom is here! Come out to meet him!’
Then all those young women woke and trimmed their lamps.
The foolish ones said to the sensible ones, ‘Let us have some of your oil; our lamps are going out.’
But the sensible ones answered, ‘No; there may not be enough for both us and you. Go instead to the dealers and buy some for yourselves.’
While they were away buying it, the bridegroom arrived, and those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut.
Later the other young women came too. ‘Sir, sir,’ they said, ‘open up for us!’
But he answered, ‘Amen, I say to you, you are strangers to me.’
Keep watch, then, for you know neither the day nor the hour.{b}
“It is like a man who was going abroad. He summoned his slaves and placed his wealth in their hands.
To one he gave five bags of silver,{c} to another two, to another one, each according to his own capability; and he went away. At once
the one who had received the five bags went and put them to work, and gained five more.
In the same way the one with the two gained two more.
But the slave who had been given one bag went away and dug in the earth and buried his master’s money there.
After a long time the master of those slaves came back and settled accounts with them.
The one who had received the five bags came forward bringing five more. ‘Sir,’ he said, ‘you entrusted five bags of silver to me; see, I have gained five more.’
His master said, ‘Excellent, good and faithful servant! You were trustworthy with a little, so I will put you in charge of much. Come and share your master’s happiness.’
The one with the two bags also came forward. ‘Sir,’ he said, ‘you entrusted two bags to me; see, I have gained two more.’
His master said, ‘Excellent, good and faithful servant! You were trustworthy with a little, so I will put you in charge of much. Come and share your master’s happiness.’
Then the one who had received the single bag came forward too. ‘Sir,’ he said, ‘I knew you to be a hard man, reaping where you did not sow and gathering where you did not scatter seed.
I was frightened, so I went off and buried your silver in the earth. There it is; take back what belongs to you.’
But his master answered, ‘You wicked, lazy servant! You say you knew that I harvest where I never planted and gather where I never scattered seed?
Then you ought to have deposited my money with the bankers, and on my return I would have got back what was mine with interest.
Take the bag from him, then, and give it to the one who has ten.
To all who have, more will be given, until they have plenty; but those who have nothing will lose even what they have.
And as for this good-for-nothing slave, throw him out into the darkness outside, where people will weep and grind their teeth.’
“When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne.{d}
All the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats.
He will place the sheep on his right and the goats on his left.
Then the King will say to those at his right, ‘Come, you whom my Father has blessed, take possession of the kingdom prepared for you since the world was founded.
For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was a stranger and you took me in;
I was naked and you clothed me; I was sick and you looked after me; I was in prison and you came to me.’
Then the righteous will answer him, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink?
When did we see you a stranger and take you in, or naked and clothe you?
When did we see you sick or in prison and come to you?’
And the King will answer them, ‘Amen, I tell you, whenever you did it for one of the least of these brothers of mine, you did it for me.’
“Then he will say to those at his left, ‘Go away from me, you who are cursed, into the everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels.
For I was hungry and you gave me no food; I was thirsty and you gave me no drink;
I was a stranger and you did not welcome me in; I was naked and you gave me no clothes; I was sick and in prison and you did not visit me.’
Then they too will answer, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not serve you?’
He will reply, ‘Amen, I tell you, every time you failed to do it for one of these, even the least, you failed to do it for me.’
And these will go away into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into everlasting life.”{e}

notes.text: Young bridesmaids: literally “virgins,” unmarried girls who would escort the bridegroom to the wedding feast with torches or lamps.
Many manuscripts add “in which the Son of Man is coming”; the Westcott–Hort text, with the earliest manuscripts, lacks it.

Bags of silver: literally “talents”; so throughout this parable. A talent was a large weight of silver, about 75 pounds (34 kg), worth about 6,000 days’ wages for a laborer, nearly twenty years’ pay. Even the one bag entrusted to the third slave was a fortune. (From this parable the English word *talent* came to mean a natural gift.)
Compare Zech 14:5; Dan 7:9–14.
Compare Dan 12:2.

verses.text: When Jesus had brought all these sayings to an end, he said to his disciples,
“You know that the Passover{a} is two days away, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.”
Then the chief priests and the elders of the people met together in the courtyard of the high priest, whose name was Caiaphas,{b}
and they laid plans to seize Jesus by cunning and put him to death.
Yet they said, “It must not be at the feast, or the people may riot.”
While Jesus was staying in Bethany at the home of Simon, known as the leper,{c}
a woman approached him with an alabaster jar{d} of very expensive perfume, and as he was reclining at table she poured it over his head.
The disciples were indignant when they saw it. “What is the point of this waste?” they said.
“That perfume might have fetched a high price,{e} and the proceeds could have gone to the poor.”
Jesus was aware of it and said to them, “Why are you troubling the woman? It is a beautiful thing she has done for me.
The poor you have with you always,{f} but me you will not always have.
When she poured this ointment over my body, she did it to make me ready for burial.
Amen, I tell you, wherever this gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her.”
It was then that one of the Twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went off to the chief priests
and said, “What are you willing to give me if I hand him over to you?” They weighed out thirty silver coins{g} for him.
And from then on he kept looking for a good opportunity to betray him.
On the first day of the festival of Unleavened Bread{h} the disciples came to Jesus and asked, “Where would you like us to make preparations for you to eat the Passover?”
He told them, “Go into the city to So-and-so and say to him, ‘The Teacher says: My appointed time is at hand. I mean to keep the Passover with my disciples at your house.’ ”
The disciples did just as Jesus had instructed them, and they prepared the Passover.
When evening came, he took his place at table with the Twelve.{i}
While they were at the meal, he said, “Amen, I tell you, one of you is going to betray me.”
They were deeply distressed, and one after another they began to ask him, “Surely not I, Lord?”
He answered, “He who dipped his hand in the dish together with me, he will betray me.
The Son of Man goes his way as it is written of him, but alas for that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had never been born.”
Judas, who was betraying him, answered, “Surely not I, Rabbi?” He said to him, “You have said it.”{j}
During the meal, Jesus took a loaf of bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to his disciples. “Take it and eat,” he said, “this is my body.”
And taking a cup and giving thanks, he gave it to them, saying, “Drink from it, every one of you;
for this is my blood of the covenant,{k} poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.
I tell you, I will not drink of this fruit of the vine again until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom.”
And after singing the hymn,{l} they went out to the Mount of Olives.
Then Jesus said to them, “This very night all of you will stumble because of me, for it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’{m}
But once I am raised up, I will lead the way before you into Galilee.”
Peter answered him, “Though all the others stumble because of you, I will never stumble.”
Jesus said to him, “Amen, I tell you, tonight, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.”
“Even if I must die along with you,” Peter told him, “disown you I will not!” Every one of the disciples said the same.
Then Jesus came with them to a plot of ground named Gethsemane,{n} and he told the disciples, “Stay sitting here while I go yonder to pray.”
He took with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, and he began to be grieved and deeply troubled.
And he told them, “My soul is ringed about with grief, enough to kill me.{o} Remain here and keep awake with me.”
He went on a little farther and fell facedown, praying, “My Father, if it can be, take this cup from me. Yet let your wish be done, not mine.”
Then he came to the disciples and found them sleeping. He said to Peter, “So, were you not able to keep watch with me for one hour?
Keep watch and pray that you may not come into testing. The spirit is eager, but the flesh is weak.”
He went away again, a second time, and prayed, “My Father, if this cup cannot be taken from me unless I drink it, then let your will be done.”
And coming again he found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy.
So leaving them again, he went away and prayed a third time, saying the same words once more.
Then he came to the disciples and said to them, “Are you still sleeping and resting?{p} Look, the hour has come near, and the Son of Man is being handed over into the hands of sinners.
Get up, let us go. Look, my betrayer has come near.”
While he was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived, and with him a large crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and elders of the people.
The betrayer had given them a sign: “The one I kiss is the man; seize him.”
He went straight up to Jesus and said, “Greetings, Rabbi!” and kissed him warmly.
“Friend,” Jesus said to him, “do what you are here to do.”{q} Then the others stepped forward, laid hold of Jesus and arrested him.
Just then one of those who were with Jesus reached for his sword, pulled it out, and struck the high priest’s servant, cutting off his ear.
Jesus told him, “Return your sword to its sheath. Those who reach for the sword will die by the sword.
Or do you suppose I could not call on my Father, and he would immediately send me upward of twelve legions{r} of angels?
But then how could the Scriptures come true, that this is how it has to be?”
At that time Jesus said to the crowds, “Am I a bandit, that you have come out with swords and clubs to take me? Every day I sat teaching in the temple, and you never laid a hand on me.
But all this has taken place so that the writings of the prophets might be fulfilled.” Then all the disciples deserted him and fled.
Those who had seized Jesus led him away to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders had gathered.
Peter followed at a distance as far as the courtyard of the high priest. Once inside, he sat down with the guards to see how things would turn out.
Now the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin{s} were seeking false testimony against Jesus so that they might put him to death,
but found none, even though many false witnesses stepped up. Finally two stepped up
and said, “This man said, ‘I am able to destroy the sanctuary of God and to build it in three days.’ ”
The high priest stood up and said to him, “Have you no answer? What is this that these men are testifying against you?”
Jesus, however, remained silent. The high priest said to him, “By the living God I place you under oath: tell us, are you the Messiah, the Son of God?”
Jesus said to him, “You have said it. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power{t} and coming on the clouds of heaven.”{u}
At that the high priest ripped his clothes{v} and said, “Blasphemy! What further need do we have of witnesses? Here and now you have heard his blasphemy.
What is your verdict?” They answered, “He deserves death.”
Then they spat in his face and struck him with their fists; and some slapped him,
and saying, “Messiah, prophesy for us: who struck you?”
Meanwhile Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. A servant girl came up to him and said, “You too were with Jesus the Galilean.”
But he denied it in front of them all, saying, “I do not know what you are talking about.”
As he went out to the gateway, another servant girl saw him and said to the people there, “This man was with Jesus of Nazareth.”
And again he denied it, with an oath: “I do not know the man!”
After a little while the bystanders came over and said to Peter, “You are certainly one of them; your accent gives you away.”{w}
Then he began to call down curses and to swear, “I do not know the man!” And at once a rooster crowed.
Peter remembered what Jesus had said: “Before a rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” He went out and wept bitter tears.

notes.text: Passover: the spring festival recalling Israel’s deliverance from Egypt (Exod 12), celebrated on the 14th–15th of Nisan, followed by the seven-day festival of Unleavened Bread.
Caiaphas: Joseph Caiaphas, high priest AD 18–36, son-in-law of Annas (John 18:13). His ossuary may have been found in Jerusalem in 1990.
The leper: presumably a man Jesus had healed, since lepers were barred from ordinary contact.
Alabaster jar: a flask of translucent stone with a long neck that was broken to pour out the contents.
A high price: Mark 14:5 says “more than three hundred denarii,” about a year’s wages.
Deut 15:11.

Thirty silver coins: literally “thirty pieces of silver,” probably shekels or Tyrian tetradrachms, about four months’ wages. Compare Zech 11:12, and Exod 21:32, where thirty shekels is the compensation for a slave gored to death.
Unleavened Bread: the seven-day festival following Passover, during which no leavened bread was eaten (Exod 12:15–20). The two were often named together.
The Twelve: the Westcott–Hort text prints “disciples” after “the Twelve” in brackets, as uncertain.
You have said it: an affirmative answer, though guarded: “It is as you say,” or “Those are your words.” Also in verse 64 and 27:11.

My blood of the covenant: compare Exod 24:8; Jer 31:31–34; Zech 9:11. Many manuscripts read “the new covenant,” as in Luke 22:20 and 1 Cor 11:25; the Westcott–Hort text, with the earliest manuscripts, lacks “new.”
The hymn: probably the second part of the Hallel (Pss 113–118), sung at the end of the Passover meal.
Zech 13:7, where Yahweh is the speaker.
Gethsemane: from Hebrew or Aramaic *gat shemanim*, “oil press,” an olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives.
Compare Ps 42:5, 11; 43:5; Jonah 4:9.
Are you still sleeping and resting? Or, as a command, “Sleep on now, and take your rest.”
Do what you are here to do: or, as a question, “Friend, what are you here for?” The Greek is elliptical.
Legions: a Roman legion had about 6,000 soldiers; twelve legions would be some 72,000.
Sanhedrin: the supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem, of about seventy-one members, chaired by the high priest.
The Power: a reverent way of referring to God without saying the name.
Ripped his clothes: a sign of grief or horror, required of judges on hearing blasphemy.
The way you talk gives you away: Galileans had a distinctive accent.

verses.text: When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel together against Jesus, to bring about his death.
They put him in chains, took him off, and delivered him to Pilate, the Roman governor.{a}
Then Judas, his betrayer, seeing that Jesus had been condemned, was seized with remorse and brought the thirty silver coins back to the chief priests and the elders.
“I have sinned,” he said, “in betraying innocent blood.” But they said, “What is that to us? See to it yourself.”
Flinging the silver into the sanctuary, he left, and he went off and hanged himself.{b}
The chief priests gathered up the coins. “We may not lawfully put these in the temple treasury,” they said, “because it is blood money.”
After discussing the matter, they bought with it the potter’s field, to bury strangers in.
That is why that field has been called the Field of Blood{c} to this day.
Then the words spoken through the prophet Jeremiah came true: “They took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one who was priced by the people of Israel,
and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord directed me.”{d}
Jesus now stood before the governor, and the governor questioned him: “Are you the King of the Jews?” Jesus said, “You say so.”
But when the chief priests and elders brought their accusations against him, he made no answer.
Then Pilate said to him, “Do you not hear how many charges they are bringing against you?”
But he did not answer him with so much as a single word, so that the governor was greatly amazed.
At the festival the governor customarily set free one prisoner for the crowd, whichever one they wanted.
They had in custody just then a prisoner of some notoriety, Barabbas{e} by name.
So when the people had gathered, Pilate asked them, “Whom do you want me to release for you, Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Messiah?”
For he knew it was out of envy that they had handed Jesus over.
While he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent word to him: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for today I have suffered greatly in a dream because of him.”
But the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus put to death.
The governor spoke to them again: “Which of the two do you want me to release for you?” And they said, “Barabbas.”
“What, then, am I to do with Jesus, the so-called Messiah?” Pilate asked them. “Crucify him!” they all replied.
“Why,” he said, “what wrong has he committed?” But they only shouted the louder, “Crucify him!”

When Pilate saw that he was accomplishing nothing, but that a riot was starting instead, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd,{f} saying, “I am innocent of this blood.{g} See to it yourselves.”
And all the people answered, “His blood be on us and on our children!”
So he set Barabbas free for them, and he had Jesus scourged{h} and handed over for crucifixion.
Then the governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the governor’s headquarters{i} and gathered the whole cohort{j} around him.
They stripped him and put a scarlet military cloak on him,
They wove a crown of thorns and placed it on his head, and a reed in his right hand. Then they knelt down before him and ridiculed him: “Hail, King of the Jews!”
They spat on him, took the reed, and kept striking him on the head.
When they had finished mocking him, they stripped him of the cloak, put his own clothes on him, and led him away to crucify him.
On their way out they met a Cyrenian{k} called Simon, and they pressed him into service to carry Jesus’s cross.
They arrived at the spot named Golgotha, that is, the Skull Place,{l}
and offered him wine mingled with gall{m} to drink; he tasted it but refused to drink.
Having crucified him, they cast lots to share out his garments among them.{n}
And they sat there guarding him.
Over his head they fixed the notice of the charge against him: THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS.
Then two bandits were crucified with him, one on the right and one on the left.
The passers-by jeered at him, wagging their heads{o}
and saying, “You who would destroy the sanctuary and build it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross!”
