In the same way the chief priests, with the scribes and elders, mocked him and said,
“He saved others; himself he cannot save! He is the King of Israel; let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him.
He trusts in God; let God rescue him now, if he wants him;{p} for he said, ‘I am the Son of God.’ ”
Even the bandits crucified alongside him heaped the same insults on him.
From noon until three in the afternoon{q} darkness lay over all the land.
And about three o’clock Jesus cried out with a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”{r}
When some of those standing there heard it, they said, “This man is calling for Elijah.”
One of them quickly ran, got a sponge, soaked it in sour wine,{s} fixed it on a reed, and offered it to him to drink.
But the others said, “Wait, let us see whether Elijah comes to save him.” [[And another took a spear and pierced his side, and out came water and blood.]]{t}
And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and gave up his spirit.
And look, the curtain of the sanctuary{u} split in two, from the top down to the bottom; the ground quaked and rocks burst apart.
The tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised;
and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they went into the holy city and appeared to many.
The centurion and his men who were guarding Jesus, seeing the earthquake and all that was taking place, were overcome with fear and said, “This man really was the Son of God!”{v}
Many women were also there, watching from a distance; they had followed Jesus from Galilee and had looked after his needs.
Among them were Mary Magdalene,{w} Mary the mother of James and Joseph,{x} and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.
When evening had come, a rich man from Arimathea{y} named Joseph arrived, who had himself become a disciple of Jesus.
He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered it to be given to him.
Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen cloth
and placed it in his own new tomb that he had carved out of the rock. Then he rolled a huge stone across the entrance of the tomb and left.
Mary Magdalene was there, and the other Mary, sitting across from the grave.
The next day, the day after the Preparation,{z} the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate
and said, “Sir, we remember that while he was still alive that impostor said, ‘After three days I will rise again.’

So give the order to have the tomb kept secure until the third day. Otherwise his disciples might come and steal him, and then tell the people, ‘He has risen from the dead.’ That final fraud would be worse than the first.”
Pilate said to them, “You have a guard.{aa} Go, make it as secure as you know how.”
So they went and secured the tomb by sealing the stone and setting the guard.

notes.text: Pilate the governor: Pontius Pilate, Roman prefect of Judea AD 26–36. An inscription bearing his name and title was found at Caesarea in 1961.
Hanged himself: Acts 1:18 gives another account of Judas’s death.
Field of Blood: called in Aramaic *Hakeldama* (Acts 1:19).

Zech 11:12–13, combined with themes from Jeremiah (Jer 18:1–12; 19:1–13; 32:6–15), which may be why Matthew names Jeremiah. In Zechariah the speaker is Yahweh, here rendered “the Lord.” The Greek follows neither the Hebrew nor the Greek Old Testament exactly. Scholarly review recommended.

Barabbas: Aramaic *Bar-abba*, “son of the father.” Some manuscripts, including Θ, family 1 and the Sinaitic Syriac, read “Jesus Barabbas” here and in verse 17, a reading Origen knew and which many scholars consider original; the Westcott–Hort text lacks it. Scholarly review recommended.
Washed his hands: a Jewish rite declaring innocence of bloodshed (Deut 21:6–9; Ps 26:6).
This blood: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Vaticanus and Bezae; most manuscripts read “this righteous man’s blood.”
Scourged: Roman flogging with a whip of leather thongs weighted with bone or metal, which often preceded crucifixion.
Headquarters: Greek *praitōrion* (Latin *praetorium*), the governor’s official residence in Jerusalem, probably Herod’s palace.
Cohort: a Roman military unit, nominally 600 soldiers, though perhaps fewer were actually present.
A Cyrenian: a man from Cyrene, a city in North Africa (modern Libya) with a large Jewish community. Mark 15:21 names Simon’s sons, Alexander and Rufus.
Golgotha: from Aramaic *gulgulta*, “skull.” The traditional English “Calvary” comes from the Latin *calvaria*, “skull.”
Gall: a bitter substance. Compare Ps 69:21 (69:22 in Hebrew). Many manuscripts read “sour wine” for “wine.”

Ps 22:18 (22:19 in Hebrew). Many later manuscripts add, from John 19:24, “in order that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.’ ”
Shaking their heads: Ps 22:7 (22:8 in Hebrew); compare Lam 2:15.
Ps 22:8 (22:9 in Hebrew); compare Wis 2:13, 18–20.
From noon until three in the afternoon: literally “from the sixth hour until the ninth hour.” Also verse 46.

Ps 22:1 (22:2 in Hebrew). *Eloi* is Aramaic for “my God”; *lema sabachthani* is Aramaic, “why have you forsaken me?” The Westcott–Hort text, with Vaticanus and Sinaiticus, reads *Elōi* here as in Mark 15:34; most manuscripts read the Hebrew form *Eli*, which better explains the bystanders’ mistake about Elijah (verse 47).
Sour wine: Greek *oxos*, cheap sour wine diluted with water, a common drink of soldiers and laborers. Compare Ps 69:21.

The words in double brackets are found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, C, L and some other witnesses, but are absent from most manuscripts, including A, D, W and Θ, and from the Old Latin and Syriac versions. They resemble John 19:34, where the piercing follows Jesus’s death. Westcott and Hort printed them in double brackets as a very early insertion, though they discussed the possibility that they are original. Scholarly review recommended.
Curtain of the sanctuary: probably the inner curtain that separated the Most Holy Place from the Holy Place (Exod 26:31–33), through which only the high priest passed, once a year.
God’s Son: or “a son of God.”
Mary Magdalene: Mary from Magdala, a town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. *Mary* is the Greek form of *Miriam*, perhaps “beloved” or “bitter”; *Magdala* means “tower.”
Joseph: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus (first hand); many manuscripts read *Joses*, as in Mark 15:40.
Arimathea: probably *Ramathaim*, the hometown of Samuel (1 Sam 1:1), northwest of Jerusalem.
The Preparation: the day before the Sabbath, that is, Friday, on which preparations for the Sabbath were made.
You have a guard: or, as a command, “Take a guard.”

verses.text: When the Sabbath was over, at the dawning of the first day of the week,{a} Mary Magdalene went with the other Mary to view the grave.
And all at once the earth shook violently; for an angel of the Lord came down from heaven, rolled back the stone, and sat upon it.
His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow.
The guards shook with fear of him and became like dead men.
But the angel spoke to the women: “As for you, have no fear. I know that you are looking for Jesus, the one who was crucified.
He is not here; he has been raised, just as he said. Come and see the place where he lay.{b}
Now go quickly and tell his disciples, ‘He has been raised from the dead, and he is going to Galilee ahead of you; you will see him there.’ This is what I have told you.”
They hurried away from the tomb, frightened yet overjoyed, and ran to bring the news to his disciples.
And suddenly Jesus met them and said, “Greetings!”{c} They came up, clasped his feet, and worshiped him.
Then Jesus said to them, “Have no fear. Go and tell my brothers to set out for Galilee; they will see me there.”
As the women went on their way, some members of the guard came into the city and told the chief priests all that had occurred.
The chief priests met with the elders and, after deliberating, gave the soldiers a large sum of money,
and instructing them, “Tell people, ‘His disciples came in the night and stole him away while we slept.’
And if the governor hears about this, we will persuade him and keep you out of trouble.”
So they took the money and did as they had been instructed. And this story has been spread around among the Jews to the present day.
The eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had directed them to go.
When they saw him, they worshiped him; but some had doubts.{d}
Jesus came near and spoke to them: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.{e}
Go, therefore, and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in{f} the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,
and teaching them to keep everything I have commanded you. And remember, I am with you every day, until the end of the age.”{g}

notes.text: At the dawning of the first day of the week: Sunday morning. The Greek may also mean “late on the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was drawing on,” that is, Saturday evening, since the Jewish day began at sunset.
Where he lay: many manuscripts read “where the Lord lay”; the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lacks “the Lord.”
Greetings: Greek *chairete*, literally “rejoice,” the ordinary greeting.
But some had doubts: or “but they hesitated.”
Compare Dan 7:14.
In: Greek *eis*, “into,” expressing entry into a relationship with the one named.
Many manuscripts add a final “Amen”; the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and others, lacks it.
